paragraphs: A molecule can be described through its two-dimensional connectivity or its three-dimensional geometry. Learning from both descriptions can produce stronger representations, but existing approaches compare them through encoded representations. The paper argues that this intermediate encoding can discard structural information that matters for connecting the two views.

MoleculeSDE instead learns to generate three-dimensional geometries from two-dimensional topologies and to perform the reverse transformation directly in the input space. It uses stochastic differential equation models with specified symmetry properties, including SE(3) equivariance and reflection antisymmetry. These properties make molecular symmetry part of the generative approach. The method also obtains a tighter bound on mutual information, the quantity used to connect information across the two modalities.

The authors compare MoleculeSDE with 17 pretraining baselines and report state-of-the-art performance on 26 of 32 downstream tasks. These results support the usefulness of its learned representations across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a stronger connection between molecular views with direct generation between those views.
icml-2023-a-group-symmetric-stochastic-d.tldr: MoleculeSDE learns molecular representations by generating between connectivity and geometry with symmetry-aware stochastic models.

paragraphs: Updating parts of an optimization problem in a fixed cycle is a natural way to use partial gradient information. Such methods are common in practice, but their theoretical behavior is less understood than that of methods that choose updates randomly. This paper strengthens the theory for cyclic updates while developing algorithms intended to scale.

The proposed A-CODER method combines cyclic coordinate dual averaging with acceleration and extrapolation. It addresses objectives consisting of two convex parts: a smooth part accessed through gradients and a possibly nonsmooth part accessed through a proximal operation. This setup lets the algorithm work with both kinds of structure while using information from blocks of variables in a cyclic order.

The authors prove an optimal convergence rate with better dependence on the number of blocks than prior work. When the smooth part is a finite sum, they also introduce the variance-reduced VR-A-CODER variant with state-of-the-art complexity guarantees. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of both algorithms.
icml-2023-accelerated-cyclic-coordinate-.tldr: A-CODER gives cyclic block optimization an optimal convergence rate and improved dependence on the number of blocks.

paragraphs: AudioLDM generates general audio from text descriptions while addressing generation quality and computational cost. Its central choice is to learn audio generation in a continuous latent representation. The system uses embeddings supplied by pretrained contrastive language-audio models, called CLAP, to connect the representations available during training and generation.

This connection allows the latent diffusion model to train using audio embeddings and then receive text embeddings as its condition when generating samples. The audio generator can therefore learn latent audio representations without itself modeling the cross-modal relationship. The paper attributes improvements in quality and efficiency to this arrangement, which separates the pretrained language-audio connection from learning to generate audio.

Trained on AudioCaps using one GPU, AudioLDM achieves the strongest reported text-to-audio performance among the open-source systems compared, using both objective and subjective measures. It also enables zero-shot text-guided audio manipulations, including style transfer. These findings show that the approach supports both generating audio from descriptions and modifying audio through textual guidance.
icml-2023-audioldm-text-to-audio-generat.tldr: AudioLDM uses pretrained language-audio embeddings and latent diffusion to generate and manipulate audio efficiently from text.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from multiple clients at a central server. Byzantine attackers can submit arbitrary gradients to disrupt this process. Robust aggregation rules attempt to defend against those updates, but the paper examines why these defenses can still fail when clients hold differently distributed data.

The authors identify two causes of degraded performance in this heterogeneous setting: high dimensionality and variation among client gradients. This matters because the server must aggregate updates in a setting where legitimate clients already produce different signals. The proposed GAS method uses gradient splitting to adapt existing robust aggregation rules to these non-IID conditions, extending the usefulness of defenses that are already available.

The paper provides a convergence analysis for combinations of GAS and existing robust aggregation rules. Experiments on several real-world datasets also support the method’s effectiveness. Together, the analysis and experiments address both the behavior of the resulting learning process and whether the adaptation helps in evaluated heterogeneous-data settings.
icml-2023-byzantine-robust-learning-on-h.tldr: GAS uses gradient splitting to adapt existing Byzantine-robust aggregation rules to clients with heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: Homotopy optimization tackles a difficult problem through a sequence of easier surrogate problems. Its effectiveness can depend strongly on how that sequence progresses, and an unsuitable continuation schedule can produce a suboptimal final solution. Traditional approaches also tend to discard intermediate solutions, even when those solutions could help with practical decisions.

This paper proposes learning the entire continuation path with a model. The path represents solutions across the continuous family of surrogate problems, including infinitely many intermediate points. Instead of moving only from easy problems toward harder ones, the approach allows the original problem and its surrogates to be optimized collaboratively. The model also supports generating a selected intermediate solution in real time.

Experiments across different problems show that the approach can substantially improve homotopy optimization performance. The learned path additionally supplies intermediate information that can support decision-making. Its value therefore lies both in improving the optimization process and in making the solutions along that process available for use.
icml-2023-continuation-path-learning-for.tldr: Learning the whole continuation path lets homotopy optimization improve solutions collaboratively and produce intermediate solutions on demand.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects an initial group of users in a social network to maximize the expected number of people subsequently influenced. Learning-based approaches offer potential for generalizing to unfamiliar graphs. Their development nevertheless faces difficulties in optimizing the selection objective, capturing varied diffusion patterns, and accommodating constraints based on node centrality.

DeepIM addresses these issues through a framework that generatively models latent representations of seed sets. It also learns different patterns of information diffusion directly from data in an end-to-end manner. This connects representations of the initial user group with the process through which influence spreads, making both parts of the problem subjects of learning.

The authors introduce an objective for inferring seed sets under flexible budgets based on node centrality. Analyses on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the framework’s overall performance. The stated contribution is a combined approach to representing candidate groups, learning diffusion behavior, and optimizing selections under different centrality-based constraints, all within the influence-maximization task.
icml-2023-deep-graph-representation-lear.tldr: DeepIM learns seed-set representations and diffusion patterns to select influential users under flexible centrality-based budgets.

paragraphs: A crystal consists of a unit cell repeated indefinitely in three dimensions. Graph representations that connect only nearby atoms do not fully capture that repetition or distant atomic interactions. This paper develops a representation for crystal-property prediction that accounts for interactions across the repeating structure.

The method models physically motivated interatomic potentials, including Coulomb attraction or repulsion, London dispersion, and Pauli repulsion, rather than relying only on atomic distances. It also considers the complete set of interactions instead of restricting attention to nearby atoms. To make this computationally workable, the authors approximate infinite sums of potentials, prove bounds on the approximation errors, and develop efficient algorithms for computing them.

The resulting potential calculations are incorporated into message-passing neural networks. Experiments on JARVIS and Materials Project show consistent improvements from using interatomic potentials and their complete versions, with reasonable computational costs. The findings support combining physically meaningful interactions with bounded approximations to represent more of a crystal’s repeating structure.
icml-2023-efficient-approximations-of-co.tldr: Bounded approximations of infinite interatomic interactions improve crystal-property prediction at reasonable computational cost.

paragraphs: Transformer policies in reinforcement learning face a difficulty highlighted by this paper: directly combining information from several imperfect trials. Agentic Transformer addresses this by organizing experience into a chain of hindsight. The training sequence contains trajectories sorted from lower to higher total reward, making several trials available together as context.

Each trajectory’s target return is relabeled to the largest total reward within that sequence. An autoregressive transformer then predicts actions using past states, actions, rewards, target returns, and task-completion tokens. This arrangement trains the model with a shared performance target across experiences of different quality. The resulting model can learn to improve upon itself during both training and testing.

On D4RL and ExoRL, the authors report performance competitive with temporal-difference and imitation-learning approaches, including when the available data is suboptimal. They also observe a promising scaling trend: larger models consistently improve results in their evaluation. These findings support learning across sequences of trials as a useful way to exploit imperfect experience.
icml-2023-emergent-agentic-transformer-f.tldr: Agentic Transformer learns from reward-ordered sequences of imperfect trials and shows competitive reinforcement-learning performance.

paragraphs: In collaborative learning with streaming data, participating organizations continually share model updates computed from newly arriving observations. Participants with more resources need incentives to contribute. Rewarding contributions fairly can address that need, but the paper observes that existing approaches can also create a rich-get-richer effect that discourages less resourceful participants.

The proposed approach first explores to estimate each participant’s contribution and then exploits those estimates to provide theoretically guaranteed fair incentives. It additionally preserves asymptotic equality: less resourceful participants eventually achieve the same performance as richer participants. Fairness concerns how rewards reflect contributions, while asymptotic equality concerns the learning performance participants ultimately reach.

The authors evaluate the approach using real-world streaming data in federated online incremental learning and federated reinforcement learning. It outperforms the compared baselines in fairness and learning performance while remaining competitive in preserving equality. These results support designing contribution-sensitive incentives together with a mechanism that keeps resource differences from determining permanent performance differences.
icml-2023-fair-yet-asymptotically-equal-.tldr: The method rewards collaborative-learning contributions fairly while preserving eventual performance equality for less resourceful participants.

paragraphs: Some prediction systems return sets of labels, and the usefulness of those sets depends on competing goals. Including more relevant labels can increase value, while incorrect predictions incur costs. The paper uses diagnosis as an example: a system should capture serious co-occurring diseases while keeping incorrect predictions under strict control.

FavMac is a general pipeline for maximizing prediction-set value subject to cost control. It can work with almost any multi-label classifier and provides distribution-free theoretical guarantees for the cost requirement. This allows the value and cost of a prediction set to be treated as separate objectives dictated by its intended use, rather than collapsing them into a single generic measure of prediction quality.

A specially designed online update mechanism makes the approach suitable for large-scale applications. Experiments on healthcare tasks and synthetic datasets show higher value than several variants and baselines while maintaining strict cost control. The results support improving useful coverage without abandoning the specified cost requirement.
icml-2023-fast-online-value-maximizing-p.tldr: FavMac builds valuable multi-label prediction sets while providing distribution-free cost-control guarantees and efficient online updates.

paragraphs: Mixup creates augmented training examples by taking weighted combinations of two inputs. Images have a shared grid that makes this operation straightforward. Graphs present a harder problem because they can contain different numbers of nodes and usually lack a direct correspondence between the nodes of one graph and another.

S-Mixup establishes that correspondence through a soft assignment matrix. Given two graphs, it uses these assignments to transform one graph’s adjacency and node-feature matrices so they align with the other graph. Once the structural and feature representations are aligned, the method can combine the graphs directly. Soft alignment therefore supplies the missing step needed to apply mixup to arbitrary graph pairs.

Experiments across graph-classification tasks show that S-Mixup can improve graph neural network performance and generalization. The authors also find increased robustness to noisy labels. These empirical findings support alignment-based graph augmentation as a way to improve learning when examples have different structures and when some training labels are unreliable.
icml-2023-graph-mixup-with-soft-alignmen.tldr: S-Mixup softly aligns nodes before mixing graphs, improving graph-classification performance and robustness in experiments.

paragraphs: Hierarchical data needs representations and distances that reflect its underlying organization. This paper introduces a method that combines diffusion geometry, an approach used in manifold learning, with hyperbolic geometry. The combination is designed to reveal hierarchical structure and then represent it in a geometric space suited to the method’s distance construction.

The first step builds densities over the data at multiple scales using diffusion geometry. These multiscale descriptions are intended to expose the hierarchy instead of representing the data at only one scale. The method then embeds those descriptions into a product of hyperbolic spaces. Both the embedding and the associated distance are central outputs of the approach.

The authors provide theoretical results showing recovery of the underlying hierarchical structure through their embedding and distance. They also evaluate the method on graph-embedding benchmarks and hierarchical datasets, reporting advantages over existing methods. The contribution links a theoretical account of hierarchy recovery with empirical evidence that the resulting representation and distance are useful.
icml-2023-hyperbolic-diffusion-embedding.tldr: The method combines multiscale diffusion densities with hyperbolic embeddings to represent and recover hierarchical structure.

paragraphs: A label-noise transition matrix describes how true labels can become corrupted. Many approaches to learning with noisy labels depend on knowing this matrix, yet recovering it without ground-truth labels is difficult. The problem becomes more challenging when the corruption process differs from one data instance to another.

This paper studies identifiability: whether the available information can determine the transition matrix. Building on Kruskal’s identifiability results, the authors establish the necessity of multiple noisy labels for instance-level identification in the analyzed setting. They also explain how additional assumptions in existing approaches alleviate that requirement. The role of those assumptions matters because identification depends on what information and structure are available.

The analysis further shows that disentangled features improve identification. This motivates a method that uses appropriately disentangled features to improve transition-matrix estimation. The contribution connects a theoretical question about when recovery is possible with a practical approach to making that recovery better, while clarifying why existing methods can succeed under additional assumptions.
icml-2023-identifiability-of-label-noise.tldr: The paper characterizes when label-noise transitions are identifiable and uses disentangled features to improve their estimation.

paragraphs: Tabular datasets can contain several views produced by different measurement sources. Traditional multi-view representation learning often assumes these feature groups share information and should be explained by globally shared factors. The paper addresses cases where dependencies are more complex and useful information is localized to particular groups.

The proposed approach represents feature sets as graph nodes and learns the edges that describe their relationships. LEGATO, its hierarchical graph autoencoder, then learns a smaller latent graph that dynamically combines information from the input views. This makes the relationships among feature groups something learned from data instead of relying on a predefined pattern of globally shared information.

Components of the latent graph specialize in information from different regions of the input. The authors report that this leads to superior downstream performance. The result supports allowing a representation to retain several localized sources of information, particularly when the assumptions used by traditional multi-view methods do not match the dependencies present in the dataset.
icml-2023-learning-representations-witho.tldr: LEGATO learns relationships among tabular feature groups and uses a latent graph to capture localized information.

paragraphs: Latent Gaussian models appear in applications including factor analysis, compressed sensing, and time-series analysis. Their classical maximum-likelihood training method, expectation-maximization, can become expensive with large datasets and high-dimensional hidden variables. The bottleneck highlighted here is the need to invert a large covariance matrix for each data point.

Probabilistic unrolling combines Monte Carlo sampling with iterative linear solvers to avoid those matrix inversions. It also unrolls the solver’s iterations so gradients can be propagated backward through the computation. This makes the sequence of solver steps part of gradient estimation for likelihood-based learning, connecting the numerical procedure directly to the training process.

The theoretical analysis shows that unrolling and backpropagating through solver iterations can accelerate gradient estimation. On simulated and real data, the method learns latent Gaussian models up to an order of magnitude faster than gradient EM, with minimal performance losses. The reported gain is a computational improvement with a small empirical tradeoff in model performance.
icml-2023-probabilistic-unrolling-scalab.tldr: Probabilistic unrolling avoids matrix inversions and learns latent Gaussian models up to ten times faster than gradient EM in experiments.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must balance reward with constraints on cost. Online training can violate those constraints while a policy learns, and practical deployments may require the policy to respond immediately when the permitted safety budget changes. This paper addresses both concerns by studying real-time budget constraints in an offline setting.

The proposed TREBI method approaches the problem through distributions over trajectories. This makes sequences of behavior the basis for handling a dynamically specified budget. Its focus is on adapting to the constraint threshold supplied in real time while operating within the offline reinforcement-learning setting, where training does not depend on collecting risky online experience.

The authors derive an error bound for estimates of episodic reward and cost, providing a performance guarantee for TREBI. Evaluations across simulation tasks and a large-scale real-world advertising application demonstrate its ability to handle changing budget constraints. The theoretical and empirical results support budget-responsive decision-making, with the guarantee specifically grounded in the analysis of offline reward and cost estimation.
icml-2023-safe-offline-reinforcement-lea.tldr: TREBI uses trajectory distributions to handle changing safety budgets in offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Self-supervised speech models have been successful for speech recognition, especially when labels are scarce. Their success has transferred less directly to tasks concerning an entire utterance, such as recognizing a speaker, emotion, or language. The authors argue that these tasks need more disentangled representations and an explicit utterance-level training objective.

Their method uses hidden acoustic units discovered through clustering to align self-supervised speech features. A factor-analysis model then applies probabilistic inference to separate underlying utterance-level representations. The same model supplies a variational lower bound that becomes an utterance-level objective. Gradients from that objective reach the transformer layers, helping them learn acoustic units that discriminate among utterance-level properties.

Combined with HuBERT’s masked-prediction training, the models outperform WavLM on every utterance-level non-semantic task in the SUPERB benchmark while using only 20% of labeled data. This result supports linking feature alignment, probabilistic disentangling, and utterance-level training to improve the evaluated speech tasks beyond word recognition.
icml-2023-self-supervised-neural-factor-.tldr: Factor analysis adds disentangled utterance representations and a training objective that improve non-semantic speech tasks with limited labels.

paragraphs: Regression residuals describe the differences between predictions and observed outcomes. This paper proposes examining those residuals through contributions associated with individual data instances. The explanatory focus shifts from asking which features account for an outcome to asking how particular observations affect the model and one another.

The proposed Shapley-based decomposition provides a model-agnostic framework for identifying instances of interest. Looking at the effects of individual observations creates an instance-level view of model behavior, including relationships among the observations themselves. This is the paper’s central explanatory move: residuals become a way to investigate the role of data points rather than only the role of their measured attributes.

The authors also connect this analysis to judging whether a model and its data are appropriate in the wider context of a study. The paper emphasizes possible applications within explainable AI and the relatively unexplored area of instance analysis. Its contribution is a framework for asking these questions and interpreting individual observations through regression errors.
icml-2023-shapley-based-residual-decompo.tldr: Shapley-based residual decomposition explains regression errors through individual data instances and their effects on the model and each other.

paragraphs: Optimization with momentum becomes computationally difficult when solutions must remain on a curved, constrained space. Maintaining that constraint can require solving difficult differential equations. This paper addresses the problem for a class of structured symmetric positive-definite matrices equipped with the affine-invariant metric, rather than for arbitrary constrained spaces.

The authors propose generalized Riemannian normal coordinates that dynamically make the metric orthonormal. In those coordinates, the problem locally takes the form of an unconstrained Euclidean optimization problem. The important qualification is local: the coordinate construction simplifies the nearby optimization geometry while addressing the original structured-matrix setting. This offers a way to reduce the geometric complications involved in momentum-based updates.

The approach is used to simplify existing methods for structured covariance matrices. It also supports the development of second-order deep-learning optimizers that avoid matrix inverses in low-precision settings. The contribution connects a geometric coordinate construction with practical optimizer design, targeting calculations that otherwise make structured positive-definite optimization difficult.
icml-2023-simplifying-momentum-based-pos.tldr: Adaptive local coordinates simplify structured positive-definite optimization and enable inverse-free second-order optimizers for low-precision deep learning.

paragraphs: Scheduling jobs across heterogeneous machines is difficult when a scheduler does not know the exact processing speed of each machine for each job. This paper studies that speed-oblivious setting and establishes strong impossibility results for both clairvoyant and non-clairvoyant algorithms. The results motivate examining what additional information can make effective scheduling possible.

The authors develop competitive algorithms for two models inspired by practice. One provides predictions of processing speeds, which may contain errors. The other provides a single global ordering of machines according to their unknown job-dependent speeds. These are different forms of partial knowledge: estimated numerical speeds in one case and a shared ranking in the other.

The paper proves theoretical guarantees for these models and evaluates the findings on a heterogeneous multicore processor. The authors describe this as apparently the first evaluation of prediction-based scheduling algorithms in a nonsynthetic hardware environment. The contribution shows how specified partial information can overcome barriers that arise when exact speeds are unavailable.
icml-2023-speed-oblivious-online-schedul.tldr: Speed predictions or a known global machine ordering enable provably competitive scheduling without exact processing speeds.

paragraphs: GENIE is a pretrained language model that generates text through diffusion. It combines an encoder with a diffusion-based decoder, which gradually turns a sequence of random noise into coherent text. The paper investigates how to pretrain this kind of generator at scale so it can support downstream text-generation tasks.

Its training objective, continuous paragraph denoise, asks the decoder to reconstruct a clean paragraph from a corrupted version. The objective encourages the reconstruction to retain both meaning and grammatical coherence. By making paragraph recovery the pretraining task, the framework gives the diffusion decoder practice restoring connected text rather than treating generation solely as a sequence of next-token decisions.

The authors evaluate GENIE on XSum, CNN/DailyMail, Gigaword, and CommonGen. It achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art autoregressive models on these benchmarks while producing more diverse text samples. The findings support diffusion pretraining as a competitive approach to the evaluated generation tasks, with diversity as an additional reported benefit.
icml-2023-text-generation-with-diffusion.tldr: GENIE pretrains a diffusion text generator through paragraph denoising, achieving competitive benchmark performance with more diverse outputs.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks, raising questions about how later learning affects earlier knowledge and overall generalization. Much existing work evaluates these effects experimentally. This paper develops a theoretical account of the factors that shape forgetting and generalization across a sequence of tasks.

Under overparameterized linear models, the authors derive explicit expressions for expected forgetting and generalization error in a setup allowing an arbitrary number of tasks. They use those expressions to explain how model overparameterization, similarity between tasks, and task ordering affect both outcomes. The linear-model assumption defines the setting in which the theoretical expressions are established.

Experiments with deep neural networks on real datasets show that some insights also carry over to practical nonlinear models. Concrete examples connect the theory to empirical observations from earlier studies and motivate improved continual-learning algorithm designs. The findings therefore offer both an analytical description in a specified model class and evidence of broader practical relevance for selected insights.
icml-2023-theory-on-forgetting-and-gener.tldr: Linear-model theory explains how capacity, task similarity, and task order affect continual learning, with some insights transferring to deep networks.

paragraphs: Learning to optimize uses machine learning to construct an optimization algorithm from data. A common approach learns the direction of each iterative update with a black-box network. Although broadly applicable, this flexibility can lead to overfitting and weak performance on problems outside the training distribution.

The paper derives basic mathematical conditions commonly satisfied by successful update rules. Those conditions guide the structure of a new learned optimizer. The approach places mathematical organization inside the model that learns the update rule, connecting the design of the learned algorithm to properties associated with effective optimization. Its goal is to retain broad applicability while improving behavior on unfamiliar problems.

Numerical simulations support the theoretical findings and show superior empirical performance for the proposed model. The authors also report good generalization to out-of-distribution problems. These results support using mathematical structure as a design principle for learned optimizers, with the observed generalization gains demonstrated in the evaluated problems rather than asserted as universal behavior.
icml-2023-towards-constituting-mathemati.tldr: Mathematical conditions on update rules guide a learned optimizer that generalizes well to out-of-distribution problems in experiments.

paragraphs: Padding in convolutional neural networks can encode absolute position information, which can harm performance on certain tasks. Understanding that effect requires reliable ways to measure how much position information the network contains. This paper argues that existing measurements are unreliable and can produce incorrect conclusions about its presence.

The authors formally define the relevant encoded information as Position-information Pattern from Padding, or PPP. They introduce metrics for measuring and visualizing it, then conduct experiments on its properties and formation. The proposed measurements detect positional information more reliably than existing approaches based on PosENet and tests used in F-Conv, giving the investigation a more dependable measurement basis.

The paper further finds that PPP is primarily an artifact of learning across existing and proposed padding schemes, with less dependence on the schemes’ underlying characteristics. This shifts the explanation toward what emerges during learning. The contribution therefore concerns both how positional information should be measured and how its emergence should be understood.
icml-2023-unveiling-the-mask-of-position.tldr: New metrics measure padding-related position information more reliably and show that it is primarily a learning artifact.

paragraphs: Kernelized Stein discrepancy, or KSD, is used to test whether observations fit a target distribution. It remains applicable when the target’s normalizing factor is unknown, which makes it useful in settings such as Bayesian analysis. This paper identifies a situation where the test can have difficulty detecting a real mismatch.

The problematic case occurs when the target and alternative distributions share well-separated modes but assign different proportions to those modes. The authors establish theoretically and empirically that KSD can have low power in this setting. Their solution perturbs the observed sample through Markov transition kernels that leave the target distribution invariant, then applies the KSD test to the perturbed observations.

Target invariance means the perturbation preserves the distribution the test is meant to recognize. Numerical evidence shows that suitably chosen transition kernels can substantially improve detection power compared with the original KSD test. The improvement is conditional on the choice of kernel, and the method directly addresses the identified difficulty with differing mixture proportions.
icml-2023-using-perturbation-to-improve-.tldr: Target-preserving sample perturbations can improve KSD test power when distributions share separated modes but differ in their proportions.
